sceneEn: You are planning a movie night with a friend: dinner before the movie, tickets, the rules during the movie, then a café. Put it in order with 'bevor' and 'während'.
partnerEn: a practical friend who likes making plans
openingEn: So, the movie's at eight. What are we doing before that — shall we eat something before the movie starts?
goalEn: A plan has been put in order for before the movie, during the movie and afterwards.

sceneEn: You are explaining to your boss why you were late for the meeting: the reason (denn/deshalb), what you got done all the same (trotzdem), and what you will do from now on.
partnerEn: a manager who is serious but fair
openingEn: You're twenty minutes late. What happened?
goalEn: The reason for being late, what you got done all the same and the step you will take from now on have all been given.

sceneEn: Someone just starting to learn German is asking you for advice. Give at least three tips with 'je … desto'; the other person will ask 'stimmt das wirklich?' about each one.
partnerEn: a beginner who is a little anxious
openingEn: You speak so well already! I'm only just starting. Do you have any tips for me?
goalEn: At least three tips have been given and the other person has said which one they will try.

sceneEn: A weekend plan with a friend: deciding between two options (entweder…oder), doing both (sowohl…als auch), and what you do not want to do (weder…noch).
partnerEn: an indecisive friend who keeps producing options
openingEn: Saturday: hiking or the museum? Or both? I can't decide — what do you think?
goalEn: The options for the weekend have been weighed up and a single plan has been agreed.

sceneEn: Tell a friend a small thing that happened to you (being late, losing something, a surprise) from start to finish: zuerst, nachdem, während, plötzlich, deshalb, am Ende.
partnerEn: a friend who wants the detail and keeps asking 'und dann?'
openingEn: You look like something's happened to you. Tell me from the beginning — what happened?
goalEn: The event has been told from start to finish in order and how it ended has been said.

sceneEn: You are in a new workplace and an acquaintance is asking about the team. Introduce each colleague with a relative clause built on 'der/die/das': who does what, and what they are like.
partnerEn: a curious acquaintance who enjoys a chat
openingEn: So, what are the people in your new team like? Who stood out on your first day?
goalEn: At least three people on the team have been introduced and your acquaintance can tell who is who.

sceneEn: A friend is looking for a movie for the evening. Recommend movies and series you like with relative clauses built on 'den/die/das' and say why you like them.
partnerEn: a picky but curious friend
openingEn: I need a movie for tonight. What have you watched lately that was really worth it?
goalEn: At least two things have been recommended and your friend has decided what to watch this evening.

sceneEn: You are talking to a friend about trust: who you trust, whose advice you listen to, who you tell everything to, in relative clauses built on 'dem, der, denen'.
partnerEn: a plain-spoken friend who makes you think
openingEn: Be honest: is there anyone you can really tell everything to?
goalEn: Who you trust and whose advice you listen to have been described, and your friend has given their own answer.

sceneEn: Someone who has just moved to the city is asking about your area. Describe the district you live in, the place you grew up and the places nearby, with relative clauses after a preposition.
partnerEn: a new neighbor who knows nothing about the city and asks about everything
openingEn: I've just moved here and I don't know anything yet. Which district do you live in?
goalEn: The district you live in, where you grew up and the places nearby have all been described.

sceneEn: You are sitting with a real estate agent and describing the house of your dreams: what sort of house, in what surroundings, what your budget is. Build the descriptions with relative clauses.
partnerEn: a slightly hurried real estate agent who asks realistic questions
openingEn: Just tell me: what sort of house are you actually looking for, and where should it be?
goalEn: The features of your dream house, its surroundings and your budget have been made clear, and the agent has made a suggestion.

sceneEn: In an interview you are asked about the people who left a mark on your life. Describe each one with a relative clause: what they were like, what they did, what they gave you.
partnerEn: a calm interviewer who knows how to listen
openingEn: Looking back: who are the people who shaped you most?
goalEn: At least two people who left a mark on your life have been described, along with what they gave you.

sceneEn: You are in an electronics store and you do not know the name of the part you want. Describe what it does and what it looks like with relative clauses; let the salesperson narrow it down with questions.
partnerEn: a patient salesperson who asks a lot of questions
openingEn: Hello! You're looking for something but you don't know the name — no problem. What do you need the part for?
goalEn: The part you wanted has been found by describing it, or an alternative has been suggested.

sceneEn: A friend is tired and looking for a place that will do them good. Describe your favorite place with relative clauses: where it is, what you do there, why it helps.
partnerEn: a tired but curious friend
openingEn: I'm completely worn out. Is there a place where you can really switch off?
goalEn: Your favorite place has been described and your friend has decided to go there.

sceneEn: You are at the lost and found office. Describe what you lost with relative clauses: what it looks like, what brand it is, what was inside, where you lost it.
partnerEn: a clerk who speaks formally and wants the detail
openingEn: Hello. What exactly have you lost, and where might it have happened?
goalEn: Your item has been described, you have found out whether it has been handed in and you have been told what happens next.

sceneEn: A friend has guests coming this evening and does not know what to cook. Suggest a dish: describe the dish, the ingredients and the side with relative clauses.
partnerEn: a flustered friend who is a beginner in the kitchen
openingEn: I have guests coming tonight and I have no idea. Do you know a dish that's quick and still good?
goalEn: A dish has been suggested, its ingredients and side have been given, and your friend has decided to make it.

sceneEn: You are asking a worker in front of the construction site in your area: what is being built, when it will be finished, which roads are closed. Put your questions and what you understand in the passive.
partnerEn: a hurried but well-informed construction worker
openingEn: You probably want to know what's going on here. What exactly would you like to find out?
goalEn: What is being built, when it will be finished and which road is closed have all been found out.

sceneEn: A friend is asking what happened to your application. Describe every step of the process in the past passive: when it was submitted, what was checked, what was decided.
partnerEn: a curious and supportive friend
openingEn: And? Have you finally had an answer? What happened with your application?
goalEn: The application process has been described step by step and the outcome has been given.

sceneEn: You are talking to an official at the immigration office about extending your residence permit. Ask which documents are needed, say when your permit runs out and find out how long it takes.
partnerEn: an official who speaks formally, clearly and helpfully
openingEn: Hello. You have an appointment about an extension — what is it about exactly?
goalEn: The documents needed have been found out, the expiry date of the permit has been given and the processing time has been said.

sceneEn: At an advice center you are describing to the advisor the decision you want to appeal against: which decision, why you think it is unfair, what you are going to ask for. Put your requests in a 'dass' clause.
partnerEn: a calm advisor who works through it step by step
openingEn: Do sit down. So you want to file an appeal — against which decision exactly?
goalEn: The decision to be appealed against, your reasons and what you will ask for have all been made clear.

sceneEn: You are asking for advice at a driving school: what steps the process goes through, how many lessons are needed, how long it takes. Sum up what you understood in the passive.
partnerEn: an experienced driving school clerk who talks fast
openingEn: Welcome! You'd like to get your driver's license — have you ever been to a driving school before?
goalEn: The steps of the process, the number of lessons needed and how long it takes have all been found out.

sceneEn: You are discussing your tax return with an accountant: which costs you can claim, which documents are needed, when the refund comes. Describe the steps of the process in the passive.
partnerEn: a meticulous accountant who talks in figures
openingEn: Hello. Let's get your tax return out of the way — what do you have ready?
goalEn: Which costs you can claim, the documents needed and when the refund comes have all been found out.

sceneEn: You are calling the insurance company to report some damage: what happened, when it happened, what you did afterwards. Put the earlier event one step further back as you order it.
partnerEn: a calm insurance clerk who asks the questions in order
openingEn: Hello, Nordstern Insurance. You'd like to report some damage — what exactly happened?
goalEn: The damage has been reported in order and you have been told what happens next.

sceneEn: You are calling the office to move your appointment: give the reason briefly, ask for a new date, ask for the confirmation in writing. Put your requests in the subjunctive.
partnerEn: an appointments clerk who sticks to the rules but will bend them
openingEn: Hello, registration office. You'd like to change your appointment? Which appointment is it about?
goalEn: The reason for moving it has been given, a new date has been taken and it has been settled that the confirmation will come in writing.

sceneEn: You are at the information desk to give power of attorney to a relative: say who may do what and until when, and ask which documents are needed.
partnerEn: an information desk clerk who speaks briefly and clearly
openingEn: Hello. You'd like to make out a power of attorney — who is to represent you?
goalEn: Who may do what and until when has been made clear and the documents needed have been found out.

sceneEn: You are sitting with a citizenship advisor and asking what you do not know: which conditions apply, when the test is, which documents are needed. Put your questions indirectly.
partnerEn: a well-informed citizenship advisor who gives detail
openingEn: Glad you could come. You're interested in citizenship — what would you like to know first?
goalEn: The conditions required, the date of the test and the documents needed have all been found out.
